title: VII. The Second Visit To Smerdyakov
paragraphs: By then Smerdyakov had been let out of the hospital. Ivan knew his new lodging: a run-down little wooden house, split in two by a passage. Marya Kondratyevna and her mother lived on one side, and Smerdyakov on the other. Nobody knew on what footing he lived with them, whether as a friend or as a lodger. It was assumed afterwards that he had moved in as Marya Kondratyevna’s fiancé and was staying for a while without paying for food or rent. Mother and daughter both respected him highly and thought him far above themselves.

Ivan knocked, and when the door was opened he walked straight into the passage. Marya Kondratyevna told him to go to the better room on the left, which was Smerdyakov’s. There was a tiled stove in the room, and it was extremely hot. The walls were cheerful with blue wallpaper, though it was badly worn, and under it, in the cracks, cockroaches swarmed in astonishing numbers, so there was a constant rustling. The furniture was very sparse: two benches along each wall and two chairs by the table. The plain wooden table was covered with a cloth with pink patterns. On each of the two little windows stood a pot of geranium. In the corner was a case of ikons. On the table stood a small copper samovar, much dented, and a tray with two cups. But Smerdyakov had finished his tea and the samovar had gone out. He was sitting on a bench at the table, looking at an exercise-book and slowly writing in it with a pen. Beside him were a bottle of ink and a flat iron candlestick, though with a composite candle in it. Ivan saw at once from Smerdyakov’s face that he had completely recovered from his illness. His face was fresher and fuller, and his hair stood up jauntily at the front and was plastered down at the sides. He was sitting in a parti-colored, wadded dressing-gown, rather dirty and frayed. He had spectacles on his nose, which Ivan had never seen him wear before. This trifling detail suddenly doubled Ivan’s anger. “A creature like that, and wearing spectacles!”

Smerdyakov slowly raised his head and studied his visitor through the spectacles. Then he slowly took them off and got up from the bench. He did it not at all respectfully, almost lazily, doing the bare minimum that common politeness required. Ivan noticed all this at once. He took it all in, and most of all the look in Smerdyakov’s eyes, which was positively malicious, surly and haughty. “What do you want, barging in?” it seemed to say. “We settled everything then. Why have you come again?” Ivan could hardly control himself.
“It’s hot in here,” he said, still standing, and unbuttoned his overcoat.
“Take off your coat,” Smerdyakov allowed.
Ivan took off his coat with trembling hands and threw it on a bench. He grabbed a chair, pulled it quickly up to the table and sat down. Smerdyakov got onto his bench before him.
“First of all, are we alone?” Ivan asked sternly and abruptly. “Can they hear us in there?”
“Nobody can hear anything. You’ve seen for yourself: there’s a passage.”

“Listen, my good fellow. What was that you babbled as I was leaving the hospital? That if I said nothing about your talent for faking fits, you wouldn’t tell the investigating lawyer our whole conversation at the gate? What do you mean by _all_? What could you possibly mean by it? Were you threatening me? Have I made some sort of deal with you? Do you think I’m afraid of you?”

Ivan said this in a perfect fury, plainly intending to show that he despised any evasion or hinting and meant to lay his cards on the table. Smerdyakov’s eyes gleamed with resentment, his left eye winked, and he answered at once, with his usual composure and deliberation. “You want everything out in the open; very well, you shall have it,” he seemed to say.

“This is what I meant then, and this is why I said it: that you knew beforehand about the murder of your own parent and left him to his fate. And that people shouldn’t afterwards draw any evil conclusions about your feelings, and perhaps about something else too—that is what I promised not to tell the authorities.”

Smerdyakov spoke without haste and plainly held himself in check, but there was something in his voice that was firm and emphatic, resentful and insolently defiant. He stared brazenly at Ivan. For the first moment a mist passed before Ivan’s eyes.
“What? What did you say? Are you out of your mind?”
“I’m in perfect possession of all my faculties.”
“Do you think I _knew_ about the murder?” Ivan cried at last, and brought his fist down hard on the table. “What do you mean by ‘something else too’? Speak, scoundrel!”
Smerdyakov said nothing and went on looking Ivan over with the same insolent stare.
“Speak, you stinking rogue! What is that ‘something else too’?”
“By ‘something else’ I meant that you, most likely, were very eager for your parent’s death as well.”

Ivan leaped up and hit him on the shoulder with all his strength, so that he fell back against the wall. In an instant his face was streaming with tears. Saying, “It’s a shame, sir, to strike a sick man,” he wiped his eyes with a very dirty blue check handkerchief and sank into quiet weeping. A minute went by.
“That’s enough! Stop it,” Ivan said sharply, sitting down again. “Don’t push me past all patience.”
Smerdyakov took the rag from his eyes. Every line of his puckered face showed the insult he had just received.
“So you thought then, you scoundrel, that I meant to kill my father together with Dmitri?”
“I didn’t know what thoughts were in your mind then,” said Smerdyakov resentfully. “And so I stopped you at the gate then to sound you out on that very point.”
“To sound out what? What?”
“Why, that very matter: whether you wanted your father murdered or not.”
What infuriated Ivan more than anything was the aggressive, insolent tone that Smerdyakov kept up all through.
“Was it you who murdered him?” he cried suddenly.
Smerdyakov smiled contemptuously.
“You know for a fact that it wasn’t me who murdered him. And I’d have thought a sensible man had no need to bring it up again.”
“But why, why did you suspect me at the time?”

“As you already know, it was simply from fear. I was in such a position, shaking with fear, that I suspected everyone. I decided to sound you out too, because I thought: if you wanted the same as your brother, then the business was as good as settled, and I would be crushed like a fly as well.”
“Wait, you didn’t say that two weeks ago.”
“I meant the same when I talked to you in the hospital. Only I thought you would understand without wasting words, and that, being such a sensible man, you wouldn’t care to talk of it openly.”
“What next! Come on, answer me, I insist: what was it ... what could I possibly have done to plant such a degrading suspicion in your mean soul?”
“As for the murder, you couldn’t have done that and didn’t want to. But as for wanting somebody else to do it, that was exactly what you did want.”
“And how coolly, how coolly he says it! But why should I have wanted it? What reason did I have for wanting it?”

“What reason did you have? What about the inheritance?” said Smerdyakov sarcastically, and somehow vengefully. “After your parent’s death there was at least forty thousand to come to each of you, and very likely more. But if Fyodor Pavlovitch had married that lady, Agrafena Alexandrovna, she would have had all his capital transferred to her right after the wedding, for she has plenty of sense. Your parent wouldn’t have left the three of you two roubles. And were they far from a wedding, either? Not by a hair’s breadth. That lady had only to lift her little finger and he would have run after her to church with his tongue hanging out.”
Ivan held himself back with painful effort.
“All right,” he said at last. “You see, I haven’t jumped up, I haven’t knocked you down, I haven’t killed you. Go on. So, in your account, I’d chosen Dmitri to do it. I was relying on him?”

“How could you help counting on him? If he killed him, he would lose all the rights of a nobleman, his rank and his property, and go off into exile. So his share of the inheritance would come to you and your brother Alexey Fyodorovitch in equal parts. You would each get not forty but sixty thousand. There’s no doubt at all that you counted on Dmitri Fyodorovitch.”

“What I put up with from you! Listen, scoundrel, if I had counted on anyone then, it would have been on you, not on Dmitri. And I swear I did expect some wickedness from you ... at the time.... I remember my impression!”

“I thought for a minute, too, at the time, that you were counting on me as well,” said Smerdyakov with a sarcastic grin. “So that was exactly how, more than anything, you showed me what was in your mind. Because if you had a foreboding about me and went away all the same, you as good as said to me: ‘You can murder my parent, I won’t stop you!’”
“You scoundrel! So that’s how you understood it!”

“It was all that business of going to Tchermashnya. Why, you were meaning to go to Moscow, and you refused all your father’s pleading to go to Tchermashnya—and then at one foolish word from me you agreed at once! What reason did you have to agree to Tchermashnya? You went to Tchermashnya for no reason, simply on my word. That shows you must have expected something from me.”
“No, I swear I didn’t!” shouted Ivan, grinding his teeth.

“You didn’t? Then, as your father’s son, you should have had me hauled off to the lock-up and thrashed for what I said then ... or at the very least given me a punch in the face on the spot. But you weren’t the least bit angry, if you please. You at once acted, in the friendliest way, on my foolish word and went away. That was utterly absurd, for you ought to have stayed to save your parent’s life. How could I help drawing my conclusions?”
Ivan sat scowling, both fists pressed convulsively on his knees.

“Yes, I’m sorry I didn’t punch you in the face,” he said with a bitter smile. “I couldn’t have taken you to the lock-up just then. Who would have believed me, and what charge could I have brought against you? But the punch in the face ... oh, I’m sorry I didn’t think of it. Even though blows are forbidden, I would have pounded your ugly face to a jelly.”
Smerdyakov looked at him almost with relish.

“In the ordinary occasions of life,” he said, in the same smug, sententious tone in which he had taunted Grigory and argued with him about religion at Fyodor Pavlovitch’s table, “in the ordinary occasions of life, blows on the face are forbidden by law nowadays, and people have given them up. But in exceptional occasions of life people still fly to blows, not only among us but all over the world, even in the fullest Republic of France, just as in the time of Adam and Eve. And they never will leave off. But you, even in an exceptional case, did not dare.”
“Why are you learning French words?” Ivan nodded toward the exercise-book lying on the table.
“Why shouldn’t I learn them, to improve my education? I might happen to go some day to those happy parts of Europe myself.”

“Listen, monster.” Ivan’s eyes flashed and he shook all over. “Your accusations don’t scare me. Say what you like about me. If I’m not beating you to death, it’s only because I suspect you of this crime, and I’m going to drag you before a court. I’ll expose you.”

“To my mind, you’d do better to keep quiet. What can you accuse me of, when I’m perfectly innocent? And who would believe you? Only, if you start, I’ll tell everything too, because I have to defend myself.”
“Do you think I’m afraid of you now?”
“Even if the court doesn’t believe all I’ve just told you, the public will, and then you will be the one ashamed.”
“That’s as much as to say, ‘It’s always worth speaking to a sensible man,’ eh?” Ivan snarled.
“Exactly right. And you’d better be sensible.”

Ivan got up, shaking with indignation from head to foot. He put on his coat and, without another word to Smerdyakov, without even a glance at him, hurried out of the cottage. The cool evening air did him good. A bright moon hung in the sky. His mind was full of nightmare thoughts and feelings. “Should I go right now and denounce Smerdyakov? But what could I say? He’s not guilty, anyway. On the contrary, he’ll accuse me. And really, why did I go off to Tchermashnya then? What for? What for?” Ivan asked himself. “Yes, of course, I was expecting something, and he is right....” And for the hundredth time he remembered how, on his last night in his father’s house, he had listened on the stairs. But now the memory brought such anguish that he stopped dead where he stood, as if he had been stabbed. “Yes, I expected it then, that’s true! I wanted the murder, I did want the murder! Did I want the murder? Did I want it? I must kill Smerdyakov! If I don’t dare kill Smerdyakov now, life is not worth living!”

Ivan did not go home. He went straight to Katerina Ivanovna, and his appearance frightened her. He looked like a madman. He told her his whole conversation with Smerdyakov, every syllable of it. She tried hard to soothe him, but he would not calm down. He kept pacing the room, saying odd, disjointed things. At last he sat down, rested his elbows on the table, dropped his head into his hands and came out with this strange statement: “If it’s not Dmitri but Smerdyakov who’s the murderer, then I share his guilt, for I put him up to it. Whether I did, I don’t know yet. But if he is the murderer and not Dmitri, then of course I am the murderer too.”

When Katerina Ivanovna heard that, she rose without a word, went to her writing-table, opened a box on it, took out a sheet of paper and laid it in front of Ivan. This was the document Ivan later described to Alyosha as a “conclusive proof” that Dmitri had killed his father. It was the letter Mitya had written to Katerina Ivanovna while drunk, on the very evening he met Alyosha at the crossroads on the way to the monastery. That was after the scene at Katerina Ivanovna’s, when Grushenka had insulted her. After parting from Alyosha, Mitya had rushed off to Grushenka. I don’t know whether he saw her, but that evening he was at the “Metropolis,” where he got thoroughly drunk. Then he called for pen and paper and wrote a document that was to have weighty consequences for him. It was a wordy, rambling, frantic letter, a drunken letter in fact. It read like a drunk who gets home and starts telling his wife or someone in the house, with extraordinary heat, how he has just been insulted, what a rascal insulted him, what a fine fellow he himself is, by contrast, and how he will make that scoundrel pay. All of it at great length, with great excitement and no coherence, with drunken tears and thumps on the table. The letter was written on a dirty scrap of the cheapest ordinary paper. The tavern had provided it, and figures were scrawled on the back. Evidently there was not room enough for his drunken wordiness, because Mitya had not only filled the margins but written the last line right across the rest. The letter went like this:

FATAL KATYA: Tomorrow I will get the money and repay your three thousand and farewell, woman of great wrath, but farewell, too, my love! Let us make an end! Tomorrow I will try to get it from everyone, and if I can’t borrow it, I give you my word of honor I will go to my father and break his skull and take the money from under the pillow, if only Ivan has gone. If I have to go to Siberia for it, I’ll give you back your three thousand. And farewell. I bow down to the ground before you, for I’ve been a scoundrel to you. Forgive me! No, better not forgive me, you’ll be happier and so will I! Better Siberia than your love, for I love another woman and you got to know her too well today, so how can you forgive? I will murder the man who’s robbed me! I’ll leave you all and go to the East so as to see no one again. Not _her_ either, for you are not my only tormentress; she is too. Farewell! P.S.—I write my curse, but I adore you! I hear it in my heart. One string is left, and it vibrates. Better tear my heart in two! I will kill myself, but first of all that cur. I will tear three thousand from him and fling it to you. Though I’ve been a scoundrel to you, I am not a thief! You can expect three thousand. The cur keeps it under his mattress, in pink ribbon. I am not a thief, but I’ll murder my thief. Katya, don’t look disdainful. Dmitri is not a thief! but a murderer! He has murdered his father and ruined himself to hold his ground, rather than endure your pride. And he doesn’t love you. P.P.S.—I kiss your feet, farewell! P.P.P.S.—Katya, pray to God that someone will give me the money. Then I will not be steeped in gore, and if no one does—I will! Kill me!
Your slave and enemy, D. KARAMAZOV.

When Ivan read this “document,” he was convinced. So it was his brother, not Smerdyakov. And if not Smerdyakov, then not he, Ivan. To him the letter at once looked like a logical proof. There could be no more doubt at all of Mitya’s guilt. It never occurred to Ivan, by the way, that Mitya might have done the murder together with Smerdyakov. In fact such a theory did not fit the facts. Ivan was entirely reassured. The next morning he thought of Smerdyakov and his taunts with nothing but contempt. A few days later he actually marveled that he could have been so horribly distressed by his suspicions. He resolved to dismiss Smerdyakov with contempt and forget him. So a month went by. He made no further inquiry about Smerdyakov, but twice he happened to hear that the man was very ill and out of his mind.

“He’ll end in madness,” the young doctor Varvinsky said of him, and Ivan remembered this. In the last week of that month Ivan himself began to feel very ill. He went to see the Moscow doctor who had been sent for by Katerina Ivanovna just before the trial. And at that very time things between him and Katerina Ivanovna became painfully tense. They were like two enemies in love with each other. Katerina Ivanovna’s “returns” to Mitya, that is, her short but violent swings of feeling in his favor, drove Ivan into a perfect frenzy. Strange to say, until that last scene described above, when Alyosha came from Mitya to Katerina Ivanovna, Ivan had not once in that whole month heard her voice a doubt of Mitya’s guilt, in spite of those “returns” he hated so. It is remarkable, too, that although he felt he hated Mitya more every day, he understood that it was not because of Katya’s “returns” that he hated him, but simply _because he was the murderer of his father_. He knew this and admitted it fully to himself.

Even so, ten days before the trial he went to see Mitya and put a plan of escape to him—a plan he had clearly been turning over for a long time. Part of what drove him was a sore spot that Smerdyakov’s remark had left in his heart: that it was to his, Ivan’s, advantage for his brother to be convicted, since that would raise his inheritance and Alyosha’s from forty to sixty thousand roubles. He decided to give up thirty thousand to arrange Mitya’s escape. On the way back from seeing him he was very gloomy and downcast. He suddenly felt that he wanted Mitya to escape not only to heal that sore spot by sacrificing thirty thousand, but for another reason as well. “Is it because I am as much a murderer at heart?” he asked himself. Something very deep down seemed to be burning and festering in his soul. His pride above all suffered cruelly all that month. But of that later....

After his talk with Alyosha, Ivan stood with his hand on the bell of his lodging and suddenly decided to go to Smerdyakov. He was acting on a sudden, odd impulse of indignation. He had just remembered how Katerina Ivanovna had cried out to him in Alyosha’s presence: “It was you, you, who convinced me of his” (that is, Mitya’s) “guilt!” Recalling it, Ivan was thunderstruck. He had never once tried to convince her that Mitya was the murderer. On the contrary, he had suspected himself in front of her, that time when he came back from Smerdyakov. It was _she_, she, who had produced that “document” and proved his brother’s guilt. And now she had suddenly exclaimed: “I’ve been at Smerdyakov’s myself!” When had she been there? Ivan had known nothing about it. So she was not at all so sure of Mitya’s guilt! And what could Smerdyakov have told her? What, what had he said to her? His heart burned with violent anger. He could not understand how, half an hour before, he had let those words go by and not cried out on the spot. He let go of the bell and rushed off to Smerdyakov. “This time I may kill him,” he thought on the way.
